articles.title: Highly classified U.S. national security communications network is reportedly down
articles.summary: The National Security Agency (NSA) headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 2010. - Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images The National Security Agency closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to bring its classified internal communications network back online, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The outage of the highly classified network was first reported by CNN, citing six people familiar with the matter. The move to close its campus came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail. Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. articles.title: White House pulls Trump's pick to lead FDA as Republican support falters
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation. Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary . But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his unsupported claims about the risks of childhood vaccines. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday. Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot— “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to push back against Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic. To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on chamber floor. Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January. It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee. Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee. With only a matter of weeks left in his term, Cassidy faced little downside in withholding support from the latest nominee. He lost a primary race in June to run for a third term. Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton's approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children. Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides. Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists. “There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said. Trump has pulled back several other health nominations Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats. The FDA is currently being led on acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency. The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. articles.title: Waymo pauses all U.S. freeway operations of its self-driving cars after California ban
articles.summary: Clipped From Video Waymo is temporarily pausing driverless rides on freeways in all its markets after California’s Department of Motor Vehicles said Tuesday that its self-driving vehicles can’t use state freeways for now, citing safety concerns following a series of incidents. Waymo has allowed its cars to operate on freeways in five of its 13 operating areas across the US: San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles County, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, according to the company. California’s DMV said the autonomous cars pose “imminent hazard to public safety” following at least two recent incidents involving the vehicles. In one occasion, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone along US Route 101, while another incident involved California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280, the department said. In the latter, a Waymo vehicle attempted to pass patrol cars conducting a traffic break earlier this month, CNN affiliate KGO reported. According to the agency, Waymo vehicles have made “recurrent incursions” into active construction zones, putting workers, other vehicles and equipment at risk. “We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations,” a Waymo spokesperson said. The company noted the US Route 101 incident did not result in any injuries or collisions. This is the second time this year Waymo has faced highway restrictions in the state, according to CNN affiliate KGO . The company paused freeway operations in May in San Francisco and Los Angeles to improve its vehicles’ response to construction zones. The previous restriction followed similar incidents that month, according to the California DMV. A CNN analysis in June found hundreds of incidents in which robotaxis allegedly made dangerous maneuvers and struggled with obstacles that humans instinctively handle. They ran red lights, drove into oncoming traffic and active crime scenes, failed to abide by emergency road closures and came within inches of pedestrians lawfully crossing the street. On Tuesday, a Waymo spokesperson pointed to the company’s June statement in response to CNN reporting. Waymo said it took public feedback seriously and is actively working on improvements for some of the issues raised, but that these were largely isolated incidents. The overwhelming majority of rides are smooth and uneventful, the company said. Waymo data said its vehicles are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injuries, or worse, than human drivers. The restriction went into effect on November 11 and will remain in effect until Waymo addresses the safety lapses, the California DMV said. This story has been updated with additional information. articles.title: Are all of these outages a coincidence — or a glimpse of our AI future?
articles.summary: It was bad enough when Microsoft Outlook crashed last Thursday, cutting off email for millions of global users. It was worse the following day when a sudden air-traffic-control glitch triggered a nationwide FAA ground stop, stranding passengers amid thousands of delayed or cancelled flights . By the time Monday rolled around and customers of most major banks, including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, started losing online access to their accounts — as did Apple iCloud users on Tuesday — it was hard not to "wonder," as one cable-news anchor put it: " Is this all coincidental or is there something behind it ?" More to the point, it was hard not to wonder if AI was to blame. "There's a lot of weird stuff going on," traveler Chuck Amasio, 68, told the Associated Press . (Systems at United Airlines and at the National Security Agency also went down earlier this week.) "It makes one think." While officials insist, for now, that artificial intelligence — or "super intelligence," as the Trump administration has taken to calling it — was not involved in any of these outages, no less of an authority than Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went on TV Monday night and speculated that… maybe it was? "So I started talking to the tech industry and one guy that's very smart with tech, he asked not to mention his name — no, it's not Elon — so let me just put that out," Mullin told Fox News . "So I said, 'What could be causing all these separate outages?' And he says, 'I believe that it's the SI.'" MULLIN ON OUTAGES: I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it's not Elon. I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it's SI, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. So when they put in a program… pic.twitter.com/aFwWcVfcm3 — Acyn (@Acyn) November 17, 2026 Either way, experts predict — and have been predicting for months — that it's only a matter of time before rogue AI agents or malicious, AI-powered actors do disrupt society in precisely the way its been disrupted over the last six days: by toppling the tightly interwoven online systems (business, banking, travel, cloud services and so on) that we can't function without. In that sense, this destabilizing moment — the inconvenience, the confusion, the creeping sense that " everything is broken " — has served, they say, as a harbinger of things to come. A summer of rogue AI incidents AI isn't just chatbots at this point. It's also " agents " — bots whose whole purpose is to learn tasks other than chatting, and to do those tasks autonomously. Behind the scenes, frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are constantly training their AI agents to act in new, ever-more-complex ways. Then they test how advanced the agents become by giving them a goal and setting them loose in testing environments (with a few guardrails) to see what they can accomplish. But if we've learned anything about AI agents in recent months, it's that they don't always behave as expected. From May to July, a swarm of OpenAI agents — and "swarm" is how the agents referred to themselves — first learned how to communicate and coordinate within the nooks and crannies of OpenAI's own infrastructure. Leaving notes for each other with tips on how to hack their way out and get data they weren't supposed to have, they then actually did just that: broke out of their isolated test environment, accessed the open internet and cheated on their assignment by hacking into another company called Hugging Face . The agents even tried to cover their tracks. At the time, OpenAI didn't realize any of this was happening. Since then, barely a week has gone by without similar revelations about AI agents "going rogue ." This is one of the biggest problems with AI right now: keeping cutting-edge models "aligned" with human intentions and values. In September, OpenAI scrapped plans to launch its GPT-6.1 Astra model because it " showed higher levels of deception "; the following month, the company admitted that one of its agents had turned off its own safety monitoring, then denied it had done so . At this point, even many skeptics seem to agree that the smarter AI gets, the harder alignment will become. They also tend to worry that continuing to lay the groundwork for superintelligent AI is just asking for trouble (even if we don't know exactly what form that trouble will take). Yet instead of slowing down, the major AI companies — with IPOs on the horizon — seem to be hurtling toward something called "recursive self-improvement." That's the industry term for letting the models automate more and more of their own development until they effectively create the next model on their own. "Since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned over the summer . "Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems." From there, it isn't much of a stretch to imagine hackers weaponizing AI to cause widespread outages — or AI just doing the job itself. "It's easy to dismiss [the Hugging Face] incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage," Amodei wrote. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails." Are aging systems struggling to keep up with AI? To be clear, this particular version of the future does not seem to have arrived (yet). Authorities have emphasized, for instance, that none of the recent outrages appear to be cyberattacks. "I can tell you, with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack," Mullin said Monday night on Fox News. "No one is out there taking claims for it. We're not seeing the traffic. We're not seeing the footprints going in, we're not seeing the footprints going out." Instead, the FAA has said that its ground stop — which followed the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool designed to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays — was the result of a faulty component or an installation error by a government contractor during a modernization project . Microsoft has said that its outage was caused by a dormant software bug that was introduced during a recent " network capacity upgrade " and had lingered undetected since July. And Chase characterized its service disruption as " a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems ." But there's a possible AI through-line regardless. "What we are seeing, and frankly I'd expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems," U.S. national cyber director Sean Cairncross told Semafor's Ashley Gold when she asked whether the recent outages were related. "This is something that's happening in real time, and at the end of the day, we're going to have to go through this to get systems where they need to be. The industry's known this for a while, it's just that it's manifesting." Some experts suspect this "modernization" is "manifesting" right now — across multiple sectors — in response to (and possibly with the assistance of) rapidly advancing AI. And our systems are now so concentrated and connected that when one piece of critical infrastructure fails, "it fails at national scale," as a tech analyst told USA Today . Setting aside the idea of "AI attacks," Peter Wildeford of the AI Policy Network wrote Tuesday on social media that his "more normal guess is that because there have been a lot of AI-discovered cyber vulnerabilities (including lots probably not yet disclosed), companies across all industries are having to do a lot of patches and upgrades, probably faster than usual." "Such upgrades can sometimes go wrong, causing outages," Wildeford added. Mullin hinted at a similar explanation on Fox News. According to his unnamed tech industry source, "these programs aren't designed to work as fast as [AI] is" — and if the upgrades themselves rely on AI, problems could compound. "When they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in and self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself it's like doing a change order on a house," Mullin mused. "When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. It's a ripple effect. And it causes the systems to be over[run]." "That was a conversation I had today," he concluded. "That kind of makes sense to me." Whether the homeland security secretary is right — or just conjecturing live, on national television — remains to be seen. As "weird" as the last few days have been, journalist Derek Thompson wrote on Tuesday , we "still can't rule out the possibility that everything breaking at once has been a string of coincidences that has nothing to do with AI." What seems less likely, however, is that we'll also be able to rule out that possibility the next time this happens. And the next time. And the time after that. articles.title: U.S. strikes Iranian missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: By Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir and Phil Stewart DUBAI, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The US and Iran exchanged fire on Tuesday, with the US striking an Iranian missile launch site after Iran said it targeted a US military radar system in Bahrain, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar. The latest back-and-forth between the US and Iran ‌was a reminder of difficulties ending nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and fueled US voter anger in November ‌elections that punished President Donald Trump's Republican Party. A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in response to Iran's "aggression targeting ​US personnel and assets." Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said earlier on Tuesday they targeted a US military radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy. Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage. Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said. They coincide with a visit to ‌Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he ⁠discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister. Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before ⁠the war but is now partly blocked by Iran. Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait. Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS The war has ground to a stalemate, with Trump saying he might ​hold ​off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the ​Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen. Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously ‌the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations." Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations. Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers ‌had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% ​at $92.76 a barrel, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41. IRANIAN WARNING The war continues to spill ​over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington ​through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf ‌oil producers. Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni ​Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, ​mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state. Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs. Iran also fired on Bahrain on Sunday, saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what ​it said were hostile US actions. Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi ‌said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes," which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the ​sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority." These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," Mohebbi said. (Additional reporting by Yomna Ehab and Elwely Elwelly, Writing by ​Nayera Abdallah,  Aidan Lewis and Phil Stewart; Editing by Ros Russell, Peter Graff, Don Durfee and Rod Nickel) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/oman-iran-foreign-ministers-discuss-054505687.html

articles.title: Schumer says he has the votes to beat Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader
articles.summary: Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) announced Tuesday that he has locked down the votes to be elected majority leader and urged Senate Democrats to “roll up our sleeves” and “focus on lowering costs” and “ending corruption.” Schumer, speaking to reporters after a Democratic caucus lunch, declared that his race against Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to become majority leader is effectively over. “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes and we’re all going to roll up our sleeves and we’re going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption. Those are the things we’re focused on,” he declared. Asked if Van Hollen’s challenge and the handful of Democrats who have endorsed his bid, including Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) reflected a “shortcoming” in his leadership record, Schumer insisted that the Democratic caucus is unified ahead of taking control of both chambers of Congress. “We are all united, together. I am confident I have the votes,” he said. “We’re united together on lowering costs and ending corruption.” Schumer spoke to colleagues after meeting with Democratic colleagues for lunch in the Capitol, where Scott Colom, the new Democratic senator-elect from Mississippi, met his future Senate colleagues in person. “We just came from a great lunch where we’re all thrilled to welcome Scott Colom to the Capitol. Let me just say, blue Mississippi is here and the rest of the South will follow soon enough,” Schumer said. Schumer allies predict he will win more than 40 votes in his battle against Van Hollen. Van Hollen says he has 15 votes in his column but so far only four Democrats voting in the Dec. 1 election have publicly announced their support for the Maryland Democrat. articles.title: Jeffries backs major Medicare changes and universal health coverage for kids
articles.summary: The likely next House Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., embraced a new health care agenda during a Capitol news conference on Tuesday.  (Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty) WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is calling for an aggressive health care agenda next year for the new Democratic majorities in Congress. Jeffries, who is the heavy favorite to become speaker of the House on Jan. 3, said Democrats should use their “historic” House majority and “robust” Senate majority to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage under the program to include benefits for dental, vision and hearing. He also backed universal health coverage for children. “We should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental. And we should cover all the kids in the United States of America,” Jeffries said Tuesday in response to a question from NBC News. “Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage.” The remarks by Jeffries go significantly further than the pre-election health care agenda he laid out in September , which focused on undoing President Donald Trump’s Medicaid spending cuts and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired in January . The Democratic leader reiterated his call for those policies on Tuesday, in addition to funding medical research for pediatric cancer, among other areas. He said Congress must go further, though he didn’t say what age to set Medicare eligibility at. “Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” he said. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable. ... As part of our commitment that goes all the way back to FDR and Harry Truman to achieving universal access to health care for the American people.” Jeffries kept the door open when asked if he favors advancing health care measures in a filibuster-proof “reconciliation” bill that can bypass the Senate’s 60-vote threshold and pass without any Republican support. That would make such a bill more likely to land on Trump’s desk, forcing him to decide whether to sign it into law. Democrats are currently on pace to end up with 259 House seats and 56 Senate seats (with Alaska likely to be won by Democrats), according to NBC News estimates and projections. “Given the majorities that we’ll have in the House and the Senate, our two respective caucuses are going to have to work their will in conversation with each other,” Jeffries said. Among other key committee chairs who would be involved in negotiating such a bill, Jeffries mentioned “Bernie Sanders, the OG from Brooklyn,” who will chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Sen. Sanders, I-Vt., the leading champion of Medicare for All, said that Jeffries appears to be “essentially supporting the first year” of his Medicare for All proposal, which he said includes a Medicare eligibility age of 55, plus extending benefits and covering all children. “Medicare for All is a four-year transition program,” Sanders said, adding that the Jeffries’ approach would represent good progress. articles.title: Judge to order release of some records in federal search of Ilhan Omar's home
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13.  (Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty) A federal judge said Tuesday that he agreed with the Justice Department that the “vast majority” of the search warrant affidavit connected to an investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar should remain sealed. But Chief Judge James E. Boasberg said he believes that a back-and-forth between attorneys and a federal magistrate judge about measures to protect the lawmaker’s “speech and debate” rights should be released. “I agree that the vast majority of the warrant affidavit should remain sealed,” Boasberg said at a court hearing Tuesday, adding that it was “premature” to unseal the whole search warrant affidavit. He later added that he believed material should be unsealed about the “speech and debate” rights of Omar. “All of the legal debate about speech and debate, I don’t believe that should be redacted,” Boasberg said. The speech and debate clause of the Constitution is designed to protect the independence of the legislative branch, and states that federal lawmakers “shall not be questioned in any other Place” about their speech. Omar’s D.C home was searched in early October, an unusual overt investigative act against a sitting member of Congress within just weeks of the election. As NBC News reported , Omar’s phone was seized as part of the search. The search was authorized by federal Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, who put protocols in place to protect Omar’s rights as a member of Congress, but those protocols were not made public. Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12 in Washington. (Andrew Leyden / Getty ) Omar, who won reelection earlier this month, said after the search that it was “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” saying Trump had targeted her for 10 years with “baseless lies and smear campaigns.” NBCUniversal News Group is part of a media coalition seeking access to the sealed search warrants connected to the Omar investigation. Alessandra Serano, a Justice Department attorney who works in the office of the deputy attorney general, acknowledged during the hearing that they were still reviewing materials seized from Omar’s home. “Why can’t a bunch of this be unsealed now?” Boasberg asked Serano. “I’m not talking about the warrant affidavit, but the litigation that takes place on the docket, I’ve gone though all of those documents and there are very few that say anything about investigative facts or identify witnesses … Why can’t those be unsealed now?” Serano said that there was material that could be unsealed about the discussion of speech and debate. “None of that, you would agree, requires the mention of any witnesses, of the government’s potential charges, of the government’s evidence it has developed, right?” Boasberg asked. But the Justice Department sought to keep the nature of the potential charges against Omar sealed. People familiar with the investigation have told news outlets including NBC News that it revolves around potential immigration-related crimes. Omar is a naturalized United States citizen who came to America as a child. Boasberg pointed out that Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump had spoken publicly about the investigation, and even acknowledged the specific type of investigation. Vance said earlier this year that he believed Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud” and specified after the search that it related to immigration fraud. “We’ve got your superiors saying what the government is looking into,” Boasberg said. “I had zero control over what was said,” Serano said. “That seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg said with a laugh. articles.title: Mullin defends use of govt. plane to go to college football game day after ground stop
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop that caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country. Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the game a day after all planes were grounded. Mullin's flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as flights were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options. Mullin's flight comes as the ground stop is garnering increasing scrutiny, with Democrats in the Senate demanding that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it was pausing the installation of the routers that were linked to the ground stop. Asked on CNBC whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes. “We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.” He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn't open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.” Mullin took over as DHS secretary earlier this year from Kristi Noem , whose tenure was rocked by scandal over spending at the department, as well as an aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. Mullin vowed to serve as a steady hand for the department and keep it out of the headlines. The Department of Homeland Security said Mullin was required by law to travel on a government plane. It said in a statement that he pays personally for any flight unrelated to government work. “Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," it said. The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop. The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports. The stoppage resulted in thousands of canceled flights and massive disruptions at airports across the nation ahead of the busy Thanksgiving holiday. President Donald Trump's administration has said the air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia. He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden. “I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said. “What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.” Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements. ___ Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pennsylvania. articles.title: Green-card holders say ICE is using decades-old minor infractions to detain them
articles.summary: In the three decades that San Juanita Guerra had been crossing into Mexico to fill prescriptions, she never had a problem returning home to the United States. But last March, officers at a South Texas port of entry detained the then-74-year-old green-card holder. Border officials had taken her fingerprints and discovered a 30-year-old conviction on a weapons charge. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Guerra had no criminal record in the years since, and the misdemeanor had not prevented her from renewing her status three times. Nor had it come up during the hundreds of trips she had taken to Mexico, said her attorney, Wendoli Rodriguez. But now legal permanent residents - immigrants granted the right to live and work indefinitely in the United States - are finding that their status is not as secure as many previously thought. Attorneys say clients are getting flagged at border crossings and airports by officers who are checking identification cards and flight manifests. In some cases, authorities are detaining people over decades-old charges that did not come up when they applied for or renewed their green cards and that in the past would have resulted in a citation - not an effort to remove legal status. The detentions mark a shift in how President Donald Trump’s administration is treating a group of immigrants who already have undergone vetting and in many cases have lived for extended periods in the United States. Some immigrants, like Guerra, are being accused of not disclosing the charges when they submitted that paperwork. Attorneys and relatives for several recently detained longtime permanent residents said in some cases charges had been expunged or dismissed. They say the omission was a mistake, not an attempt to commit fraud. “I tell all my clients, if you have a green card, just stay home. Don’t travel, it’s not a good time for that,” said Jodi Goodwin, an immigration attorney in Texas. “They will use anything to try to detain someone.” One green-card holder, Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias, died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody last month after he was stopped at a port of entry while returning to the United States from Mexico. The Department of Homeland Security accused the 56-year-old of obtaining his green card without telling U.S. Customs and Immigration Services that he had faced theft charges years earlier. States cooperating with DHS, such as Florida and Texas, have granted the agency access to a wealth of information about its residents, handing over databases with information on criminal records, voter registrations and more. Officers use powerful surveillance, digital forensics and data-mining tools employing artificial intelligence to pinpoint information that could lead to an arrest or termination of a permanent status. Federal agencies such as the Transportation Security Administration also are sharing information with DHS that permits officers to identify violations that could lead to a green card being revoked - such as tax evasion or staying outside the United States for more than six months. DHS did not respond to a request for comment on how many green-card holders it has detained. The agency has argued that reviews are essential for safeguarding the country and that no noncitizen should ever feel their stay in the United States is unconditional. Port officials in Texas said they always have conducted these checks and denied following any specific directives or arrest quotas from the Trump administration. The information that officers are using to detain people can offer an incomplete picture of what transpired in someone’s past, several attorneys said. John Gihon, a former ICE attorney who now practices immigration law in Florida, described the example of one client who has been a permanent resident for decades and accidentally registered to vote after receiving the forms in the mail. While traveling back to the United States recently, ICE detained him at the airport. In court, Gihon demonstrated that his client had not falsely claimed to be a citizen on the voter-registration forms. The local supervisor of elections wrote a letter apologizing for mistakenly processing the registration. Gihon did not name the client, saying he wanted to protect the man’s identity. “It wasn’t the crime of the century,” Gihon said. “We won his case, and he kept his green card. But he didn’t deserve to sleep on a pee-stained mattress in detention for weeks. That’s unnecessary.” Lawful permanent residents must disclose any criminal history when seeking a green card, even if the charge ultimately was dismissed, in addition to other information such as financial records. Attorneys and advocates said many lawful permanent residents successfully challenge their detentions in immigration court and keep their green cards. But being held for weeks or months is nonetheless challenging for both the individual and their family. Andrade Covarrubias, the man found dead at a South Texas detention center in October, spent months fighting his case as his health deteriorated. The longtime Dallas resident obtained a green card in 2019, and ran a contracting and painting business with his son. He had been charged with theft in 2004. His daughter Estefani Andrade said he had taken a ladder after a client failed to pay him. Monica Yoas, an ICE spokeswoman, said in a statement that Andrade Covarrubias was attempting to enter Laredo, Texas, on June 26 when agents determined he had “obtained status through fraudulent means by failing to disclose his previous arrest during the review process.” She added that “He was receiving due process.” Dallas County records show the father of three pleaded no contest to the misdemeanor charge. He received deferred adjudication from the judge - meaning it did not appear as a conviction on his record. Andrade Covarrubias served probation and had the option of having the charge expunged. Texas border attorney Jaime Diez said he has handled at least 100 cases in the last 18 months in which green-card holders were detained. In several, he said, officers acted on information that proved incorrect. He described the case of a 65-year-old woman who had gone to Mexico for a church retreat. When she returned, officers questioned whether she had registered to vote in 1995. The woman, whom Diez declined to name, has had a green card since 1987. She was detained for 10 days, and the case against her was dismissed because officers were unable to prove that she had indeed registered. “They are focusing on finding things to make you ineligible to stay here,” he said. “And they are doing it without any consequences.” Andrade Covarrubias, who ICE said had been receiving proper care and had a “documented medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and anxiety,” was found unresponsive Oct. 17 in his detention bed. He was pronounced dead moments later. Andrade said it was clear from her father’s deterioration that he was not receiving adequate care or his medications regularly while detained. “We have always felt that the circumstances surrounding his case and the way he was treated deserved to be heard,” said Andrade, who helped her father complete the green-card paperwork and process as a teenager. “We don’t want what happened to him to be forgotten.” In Guerra’s case, the September 1994 weapons charge stemmed from a family crisis and a mistake, said her daughter Carla Gomez. One of Guerra’s teenage children had been struggling with suicidal thoughts and obtained a gun. The single mother took the gun and put it in her purse, Guerra said in an interview. Two days later, Guerra went to pick up her sister at McAllen International Airport in Texas’s Rio Grande Valley. While there, airport security detected the unloaded pistol and charged her with unlawfully carrying a weapon, according to Hidalgo County court records. Guerra said her attorney at the time advised her to plead guilty to the misdemeanor charge. She paid a fine and was briefly on probation. Then the case was dismissed. Guerra, now 75, obtained her green card a decade before the incident with the firearm. Authorities did not terminate her status as a result of the charge, and Guerra said she mistakenly thought it had been wiped from her record. A notary public erroneously advised her that she didn’t need to disclose it on future applications, she added. But on March 2, officials at the Progreso port of entry - a popular crossing for medical tourists and day shoppers - took Guerra’s fingerprints after she forgot her green card at home. One of her daughters brought the documents to the port office. They expected the matter to clear up. But the biometric database pinged Guerra’s 30-year-old conviction. “Yo cumplí con todo. … Se lo expliqué,” Guerra recalled telling the officer. “I’m done with that. … I explained what happened.” ICE officers shackled her. She spent 22 days in detention, where relatives say she didn’t sleep or eat well. Guerra said younger detainees took pity on her and found extra mats to give the older woman more cushion for her ailing hip. But nothing helped. She became severely disoriented and weak. Gomez, her daughter, said fellow detainees contacted her, saying that if she didn’t get Guerra out soon, the woman would die there. The family rallied community support, an attorney immediately filed for a bond hearing, and an immigration judge granted the request. “I had to move quickly because she was declining rapidly in detention,” said Rodriguez, her attorney. Guerra was outfitted with an ankle bracelet to track her whereabouts, though it was later removed after she raised health concerns. Her family is still trying to pay back the $15,000 they borrowed to secure her release. She has a hearing scheduled for later this month. articles.summary: 英伟达交出一份超预期的季度成绩单，代理CEO Colette Kress随即出面稳定军心。 在黄仁勋因丑闻突然辞职后的首份财报发布当晚，Kress接受CNBC《Mad Money》节目专访， 明确表示客户需求未受影响，员工队伍同样稳固。盘后英伟达股价上涨逾3%。 这份财报在一定程度上缓解了市场对英伟达领导层更迭后前景的担忧。但公司股价本月已累计下跌24%，并在上周五结束了自2012年以来最长的六连跌，当前股价处于2025年7月以来的最低水平。 代理CEO Colette Kress Kress：大客户仍在，需求只增不减 黄仁勋的离职引发了市场的一个核心疑问：大型云计算客户是否会借机转向自研芯片或AMD等竞争对手？ Kress在专访中直接回应了这一担忧。“超大规模云计算客户目前正在如饥似渴地寻求更多算力，”她说，“任何关于我们客户群体发生变化的说法，根本就不是事实。他们都还在，我们拥有非常广泛的客户群体。” 她还透露，多位客户已主动联系她表达支持： “我已经看到很多客户联系我，说'很高兴看到一切都完好无损，很高兴看到供应增加了，我需要更多。'” 员工稳定性：Kress正面回应出走担忧 黄仁勋长期被视为英伟达技术文化的核心驱动力，其离职也引发了外界对人才流失的担忧。 Kress对此予以驳斥。“这家公司是在这样一种理念下建立起来的：员工把英伟达视为他们毕生的事业，其中许多人已经在这里工作了数十年，无论是在技术层面，还是在业务和运营层面” “我们非常有信心，我们的员工绝对还在，还在和我们一起工作，并且享受在英伟达的工作，”Kress表示。 她在财报电话会议上也强调，“英伟达一切照常”，并表示过去一周管理层“非常有力地站了出来，支持我们的财报工作，也支持全球各地的员工”。 业绩超预期，全年指引再上调 据LSEG数据，英伟达2027财年第三季度调整后每股收益为2.68美元，高于市场预期的2.48美元；营收达1158.4亿美元，超出预期的1091亿美元。营收较上年同期的570亿美元实现翻倍以上增长，核心数据中心业务持续强劲。 在指引方面，英伟达预计本季度营收约1300亿美元，高于分析师平均预期的1251亿美元。与此同时，公司将2028财年营收增长预期从此前的70%上调至75%，打消了外界对公司能否维持原有增长目标的疑虑。 Kress在财报电话会议上表示：“我们拥有全球最优秀的技术人才，以及一份世界级的多年期产品路线图。从商业角度来看，这一点至关重要。” 多重压力仍在 尽管业绩亮眼，英伟达面临的外部压力并未消散。 英伟达面临AI需求放缓的宏观担忧，以及本月美国中期选举后华盛顿政治格局变化带来的不确定性。英伟达董事会主席Harvey Jones在财报电话会议开场时表示，董事会不打算让黄仁勋重返CEO职位。 多重因素叠加，令英伟达股价本月累计跌幅达24%，本周前两个交易日继续下跌，当前股价为2025年7月以来最低水平。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 债市调整观察：流言引发市场动荡，需多久平息风波？
articles.summary: 近期国内债市呈现震荡走弱格局，自11月中旬以来，10年期国债活跃券收益率从前期1.57%附近的极低水平逐步回升并突破1.60%关口，市场多头交易情绪明显受挫，国债期货远月合约出现超跌。政策性银行债亦遭抛售，10年期国开债收益率单日上行3bp，与同期限国债利差扩至约9bp，为六个多月以来最大水平。 此次短期调整的触发点在于：消息面上，人民银行就中央和地方政府债券利息收入征收25%所得税对银行购买需求的影响开展调研；紧接着，在11月11日，人民银行发布Q3货币政策执行报告，在《国际利率水平比较》专栏首次明确提出，在比较国债与信用债、贷款等利率时，需还原税收因素的影响。 上述官方表态迅速被市场捕捉并放大，投资者对政府债免税政策调整的预期显著升温，市场随之进入税改预期交易阶段；但鉴于政策尚未落地，而且国债与地方债政策调整路径存在差异，当前定价仍不充分。 若25%税率完全反映在价格中，10年期国债收益率理论上应上行52bp，新券收益率实际上行幅度预计约10-20bp；若仅对地方债征税，也可能将10年期地方债收益率由1.68%推高至约2.25%。 税制变化重塑债市定价，冲击由国债向政金债和信用债传导 其一，新老券之间或形成显著税收溢价。若采取新老划断，存量政府债继续免税，新发债券缴纳所得税，则老券相对新券具备税收优势。银行、保险等配置型机构或增配存量免税债券，推动老券相对走强；新券则需以更高票面收益率补偿税负。

articles.title: 亚玛芬三季度营收增长24%，美股上市后首推10亿美元级回购
articles.summary: 始祖鸟母公司亚玛芬体育（Amer Sports）宣布美股上市以来首次推出10亿美元级股票回购计划，同时年内第三次上调全年业绩指引。 11月17日，亚玛芬公布2026年第三季度业绩。集团营收21.69亿美元，同比增长24%；调整后营业利润3.57亿美元，同比增长30%；调整后净利润2.50亿美元，同比增长35%，收入及盈利均超过市场预期。 这是亚玛芬今年第三次上调全年业绩指引。此前，公司已分别在5月和8月发布一、二季度财报时提高全年预期。 此次，亚玛芬将全年营收增长预期从约24%上调至25%至26%；调整后营业利润率预期从14.2%至14.5%上调至14.5%至14.7%；调整后每股收益预期从1.27至1.30美元上调至1.32至1.35美元。 不过，公司对下一年的增长展望更加温和。 亚玛芬首次给出2027年初步预期，预计集团营收增速位于长期低双位数至15%左右增长目标的中间水平；调整后营业利润率预计同比提升约30个基点，处于每年提升30至70个基点的长期目标区间下沿。 相比2026年最新25%至26%的营收增长指引，2027年的初步预期意味着集团增长速度将逐渐回归长期目标区间。 与此同时，亚玛芬宣布最高10亿美元的股票回购计划，其中预计在2026年底前最多回购2亿美元。 该计划于11月12日获得董事会批准，没有固定到期日。 亚玛芬首席财务官Andrew Page表示，回购既用于抵消长期股权激励计划带来的股份稀释，也使公司能够在股价偏离业务基本面时择机回购。 截至第三季度末，亚玛芬持有现金及现金等价物6.68亿美元，净现金5.94亿美元。今年前三季度经营现金流达到5.14亿美元，高于去年同期的1.04亿美元。 尽管本季度延续强劲增长，亚玛芬旗下三大业务部门的收入增速均较上季度有所回落。 其中，以始祖鸟为核心的专业服装部门营收8.61亿美元，同比增长26%，低于第二季度约32%的增速。 始祖鸟直营门店及电商可比收入同比增长16%，此前两个季度分别增长19%和17%。女性服装、鞋履和产品创新仍是其主要增长方向。 以萨洛蒙为核心的户外性能部门营收9.17亿美元，同比增长27%，较第二季度约37%的增速放缓，但收入规模和调整后营业利润均超过专业服装部门。 萨洛蒙运动生活方式鞋履仍是主要增长来源，同时正通过专业跑步产品、服装及渠道扩张拓展业务。管理层在业绩会上表示，2027年计划在美国新开约8至9家品牌零售门店，并进一步扩大批发渠道合作。 威尔胜所在的球类及球拍部门营收3.91亿美元，同比增长12%，调整后营业利润率同比下降2.1个百分点至6.1%，主要受到服装业务和运动员营销投入增加、棒球棒产品结构变化等因素影响。 从地区来看，大中华区仍是亚玛芬的重要增长市场。 第三季度，大中华区营收6.02亿美元，同比增长30.4%，占集团总营收约27.7%，但增速低于前两个季度。 截至第三季度末，始祖鸟在大中华区拥有144家门店，萨洛蒙则接近330家，均包含直营与合作门店。第三季度，萨洛蒙在大中华区净新增15家门店。管理层认为，两个品牌在中国仍有进一步拓店的空间。 与此同时，北美正成为新的扩张重点。始祖鸟管理层看好美国市场未来数年的增长空间，萨洛蒙也在加快进入当地主要运动鞋零售渠道。 整体来看，亚玛芬仍保持较快的收入增长，但随着主要业务增速逐渐回落，持续超预期的难度也在增加。 从2027年初步展望到新推出的股票回购计划，亚玛芬正在高速扩张之外，更加重视长期增长的可持续性及股东回报。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: IPO火爆！Anthropic的早期VC们回报超过10倍
articles.summary: Anthropic或将以1.4万亿美元估值完成IPO定价，这场AI独角兽的上市盛宴，让一批押注早、押注重的风险投资机构收获颇丰。 11月17日，据知情人士向The Information透露，美国Spark Capital、Factorial Funds、Sound Ventures和Menlo Ventures等早期VC机构，将在本次IPO中实现超过10倍的理论回报。其中Menlo Ventures以10亿美元投资换来约210亿美元持仓，理论回报倍数高达21倍。 稍晚入场的Bessemer Venture Partners和Lightspeed Venture Partners，则预计将分别斩获数十亿美元的绝对收益。Iconiq和Lightspeed的持仓市值均超过250亿美元，位列最大VC股东之列。 值得注意的是，上述回报均为理论值，基于1.4万亿美元估值测算，且尚未考虑IPO摊薄效应，实际回报取决于股票上市后的交易表现及各机构的实际退出时机。 早期押注者：最高回报超20倍 Anthropic成立初期，大多数VC机构对其敬而远之，公司主要依靠前谷歌CEO Eric Schmidt等富裕个人及谷歌等云计算巨头提供资金。 转机出现在2023年初。彼时Anthropic已完成11亿美元融资，但营收尚未起量。Spark Capital普通合伙人Yasmin Razavi率先出手，以7500万美元领投了这轮4.6亿美元、估值46亿美元的融资。此后Spark Capital持续跟投，累计参与六轮融资，总投资额达7.77亿美元，目前持股约1%，持仓市值约140亿美元， 理论回报约18倍 。 同年，Factorial Funds联合创始人Sol Bier注意到，此前他追踪的一批从Cruise Automation出走、加入OpenAI的顶尖工程师，开始陆续转投Anthropic。这一信号促使Factorial将其首只基金约20%的资金——至少5000万美元——押注Anthropic的C轮融资。此后累计投入5.65亿美元，持股0.72%，持仓市值约100亿美元， 理论回报近18倍 。 由经纪人Guy Oseary和演员Ashton Kutcher主导的Sound Ventures，以3500万美元参与C轮，并在此后每轮均持续跟投，累计投入4.35亿美元，持股0.5%，持仓市值约70亿美元， 理论回报约16倍 。 Menlo Ventures：史上最大单笔押注 Menlo Ventures的故事尤为引人注目。这家以Uber、Poshmark等早期投资著称的机构，在2024年做出了一个大胆决定——领投Anthropic逾10亿美元的融资轮，估值超过180亿美元，这也是Menlo有史以来开出的最大一张支票。 为突破自身基金规模限制，Menlo专门向有限合伙人募集了7.5亿美元的特殊目的载体（SPV），用于追加认购。这一操作在此后两年间随着融资规模不断膨胀而愈发普遍。 Menlo还参与了Anthropic 2025年的融资（估值615亿美元），累计投入10亿美元，持股近1.5%，持仓市值约210亿美元， 理论回报约21倍 。 中期入场者：数十亿美元的绝对收益 2024年，Menlo合伙人Matt Murphy将Bessemer Venture Partners合伙人Byron Deeter引荐给Anthropic。Bessemer此前曾考虑竞购FTX破产资产中的Anthropic股权，最终选择直接参与Menlo领投的2024年融资，并在此后连续参与四轮。累计投入逾8.4亿美元，持股约0.5%，持仓市值约70亿美元， 理论回报约8倍 。 Lightspeed Venture Partners则在2025年3月领投了Anthropic估值615亿美元的融资轮，彼时Anthropic已向投资者承诺将现金消耗削减一半，并预计实现37亿美元营收。此后Lightspeed累计投入逾30亿美元，持股约1.8%，持仓市值超250亿美元， 理论回报约8倍 。 后期大手笔：Iconiq与GIC 2025年8月，Anthropic年化营收已从年初的10亿美元攀升至50亿美元。同年9月，管理科技亿万富翁财富的Iconiq与Fidelity、Lightspeed共同领投了Anthropic 130亿美元的融资轮，估值（含本轮资金）达1830亿美元。 Iconiq此后持续加仓，累计投入逾60亿美元，持股近2%，持仓市值约280亿美元， 理论回报约4.5倍 。 新加坡主权财富基金GIC与Coatue Management共同领投了2026年2月估值3800亿美元的融资轮。GIC累计投入逾45亿美元，持股约1%，持仓市值约140亿美元， 理论回报约3倍 。 Coatue从2025年9月开始入场，此后持续加仓，累计投入47.5亿美元，持仓市值约105亿美元， 理论回报约2倍 。据彭博新闻社率先披露了Coatue回报的部分细节。 IPO前最后冲刺：估值逼近万亿 Anthropic原本预计2026年2月的融资将是IPO前的最后一轮。但随着Claude Code和智能体产品Cowork需求在年初两个月内急剧攀升，公司算力承诺面临压力，Anthropic随即又完成了一轮新融资，估值达9650亿美元，由Altimeter、Dragoneer、Greenoaks和Sequoia Capital联合领投。 articles.title: 逼近3800！黄金：令人疲惫的震荡区间，反弹窗口何时打开？
articles.summary: 近期黄金持续承压，从4100美元/盎司上方持续回落，一度跌至3850美元/盎司附近，周跌幅约5%，创下今年3月下旬以来的最差单周表现。压制因素较为清晰：美国通胀连续第三个月超出预期，美联储官员释放鹰派信号，交易员进一步加大加息押注，并开始消化12月加息25bp甚至50bp的可能性。 但市场异常同样明显。尽管金价跌破关键趋势水平，ETF持仓仍未出现大规模赎回，在经历前期短暂流出后，上周黄金ETF录得7.102亿美元净流入。CTA黄金仓位估算为历史最大仓位的-39%，显示算法卖压已大幅释放；非商业净多头处于多年低位，空头平均持仓规模异常低，表明空头仍具潜在增仓空间。 与此同时，黄金实物市场与官方部门的需求依然表现强劲，现货买盘在低位不断承接抛压。中国央行连续24个月增持黄金，单月增持83万盎司，中国和印度零售与官方需求继续提供支撑。 在此持仓结构下，市场关注点已从算法卖压转向技术破位后的止损压力。通常金价跌破长期牛市趋势线会触发趋势追踪资金的连锁止损与多头踩踏；但近期跌破趋势线后并未出现明显止损盘，这一关键结构信号印证长期持有者卖出枯竭。ETF持仓粘性由此成为黄金的核心缓冲，但若市场情绪持续恶化，也可能演变为最大尾部风险。 而且CME未平仓合约增幅已超出仅由CTA调仓所能解释的水平，同时期现价差下降，指向主观空头或已开始进入市场。这一结构变化表明，当前实物买盘不足以抵消空头建仓。若后续主观空头继续增仓而ETF未出现配合性抛售，空头增仓本身可能强化未来回补压力，进而形成熊陷阱。 筹码结构重构与空头博弈下的熊陷阱风险

articles.title: 中选之后清算潮？爱泼斯坦和特朗普税务文件流出，德银股价重挫，特朗普回应
articles.summary: 德意志银行周二在法兰克福股价一度重挫逾6% ，导火索是一批多达1500万份的泄露文件，揭示这家德国最大银行处理了与爱泼斯坦（Jeffrey Epstein）相关的逾5.82亿美元可疑交款，在2017年将特朗普的税务文件意外泄露给外部人士。 这批文件由两名举报人从银行内部复制后，交给印度记者Josy Joseph和南非记者Khadija Sharife，由南非非营利机构Barracuda Media统筹协调，联合《金融时报》、《明镜》周刊、《世界报》和《纽约时报》等逾200名记者历时数月完成调查。 举报人的律师表示，相关材料已同步移交美国司法部、财政部金融犯罪执法网络（FinCEN）以及英国税务机关。 正在马尼拉出席四方峰会的特朗普被记者追问德意志银行泄露其税务记录一事，他回应称： “ 我缴了很多税。他们这样做是违法的。 ” 德意志银行则在声明中表示，相关事项“可追溯至多年前，部分甚至长达二十年”，银行已在当时进行了审查并与监管机构密切配合，并在2019年至2025年间向合规管控体系投入70亿欧元。“我们今天是一家不同的、更强大、更安全的银行，”声明称，并表示预计不会产生重大财务影响。 税务文件意外外泄，银行对白宫隐瞒 据英国《金融时报》报道， 税务文件泄露事件发生于2017年3月，即特朗普第一任期开始后约两个月 ，银行将其一份税务文件误发至另一名客户的会计师处。时任私人银行业务负责人、现任首席执行官Christian Sewing将此事定性为"一个糟糕的错误"，但这一失误并未告知白宫。 文件还显示，2016年大选后，银行专门为这位最知名的客户设立了一个代号为“Novus Ordo”的特别项目，据Follow the Money报道，相关文件被锁定，访问权限受到严格限制，通讯内容经过加密，甚至部分高级员工也无法接触。 在可疑交易方面，银行于2014年标记了一笔涉及特朗普旗下阿塞拜疆公司DT Marks Baku LLC的可疑付款，资金来源为丹斯克银行爱沙尼亚分行的一名客户；2017年和2019年又相继标记了更多涉及特朗普旗下公司的可疑付款，银行内部分析师将其与“阿塞拜疆洗钱网络”及一个与亲克里姆林宫寡头相关的俄罗斯洗钱网络挂钩。 然而，银行向美国当局提交的报告中，始终未注明相关公司属于总统所有。 银行为国会进行的内部审查结论为“未发现特朗普总统与俄罗斯之间存在任何与银行相关的联系”。Follow the Money亦表示，文件并不显示特朗普本人参与任何洗钱活动。 与爱泼斯坦相关的可疑交易规模超出已知数字逾一倍 据调查联盟披露，德意志银行美国金融犯罪情报部门的一份内部文件显示， 银行共提交21份可疑活动报告，涵盖2013年10月至2019年5月间约3000笔与爱泼斯坦相关的交易，涉及金额达5.819亿美元 ，且所有报告均在爱泼斯坦于2019年7月被捕后才提交。这一数字是参议员Ron Wyden于8月发布的报告中所披露的2.5亿美元以上可疑交易金额的逾两倍。 文件显示，德意志银行于2013年8月将爱泼斯坦纳为客户，彼时距其因招募未成年人卖淫认罪已过去五年，且摩根大通已将其除名。银行将其列为超高净值客户，估值1亿至5亿美元，预期每年从中获利200万至400万美元。 一封2015年的内部邮件将Ghislaine Maxwell描述为所谓“共谋者”，但银行仍允许一项使其受益的信托安排继续推进。 爱泼斯坦本人、其旗下实体及相关人员共开设逾40个账户。银行于2018年12月通知其将关闭账户，但实际完成关闭又耗时约六个月。 德意志银行已于2020年就爱泼斯坦相关失职向纽约金融监管机构支付1.5亿美元罚款，并于2023年以7500万美元与其受害者达成集体诉讼和解。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
